newsitem.title: UK: Beloved firebrand of the British left.
newsitem.headline: Beloved firebrand of the British left.

text.p: She is the most popular woman in her party. Known for speaking her mind, consequences be damned, this is a politician who is both loved and loathed.
Few faces are as familiar on the British election scene and even fewer mouths have her knack for courting controversy.
She is not Margaret Thatcher, that standard bearer of the right, but Clare Short, firebrand of the Labour left.
Comparisons with the former prime minister are not welcome.
"She's history," said Short dismissively, revving up her car for another day's campaigning in her native Birmingham.
"The values that have been celebrated over the past 20 years, I find repulsive."
Short is a near-certainty to retain her ethnically-mixed Midlands constituency in Thursday's election, when the Labour Party is also expected to win power nationally after 18 years in waiting.

Thatcher can only preach from the sidelines these days, while Short wins adulation on the streets of Birmingham and constant attention in the national press, ever watchful for any slip-up or overly candid comment.

Indeed, with Thatcher ever more smitten with the far right and Short a lifelong leftist, the two women's similarities are about conviction and that alone. Both share an unflinching belief in self, a deep commitment to their own brand of politics and an ability to win headlines and turn heads without trying.
"You have to proceed on the assumption that people know who you are," she said.
"But you mustn't get the disease of some MPs where you walk though the door and pause, awaiting all that recognition."
All in all, it is very hard not to like Short, a woman with wit and guts and warmth, dubbed "Labour's loose cannon" and a charter member of its "awkward squad" by a suspicious press.
At 51, this rebel with a cause is working hard to stay out of trouble in the final countdown to election day.

She has visited 26 constituencies to lend support to struggling candidates. And she has tried to avoid the sort of overt criticism of her own party that led to her demotion last year from Labour's transport portfolio to overseas development.

Short was "hurt" at the time -- she had lashed out with passion at Labour's powerful new spin doctors -- but insists she is now happy in her work and is neither a martyr nor loose-lipped, just honest. Too honest for her own good?
"No. I do want to be able to talk honestly in plain language. But it's not heroic. And I don't agree that I'm gaffe-prone," said Short.

"I despise this. We're in this stranglehold period where everyone says they want honesty but the way the media works, it's impossible. So the politicians speak in sound-bites, which everyone hates, and they're trying to drive me into that too."
CANDID CLARE
Few expect Short to be driven into sound bites, silence or anything else she doesn't like.
Indeed, even on best behaviour, Short can't resist a jibe at those within so-called New Labour who wish for less candour on her part and more parroting of the centrist New Labour line.

Why is it, Short wonders with characteristic mischief, that she has only spotted Labour's stern "Young Offenders Will Be Punished" poster hanging in her own constituency and nowhere else. Is the party leadership trying to tell her something?
"Everyone says they like me because I'm genuine," says Short. "But it's such a hard business. Black moments are plentiful -- there are easier ways to earn a living."
To be hounded for any slip of the tongue, flash of honesty or out-of-context word, she says, "is a terrible burden".
Yet the former Catholic is quick to dismiss suggestions that s a saint to the cause of truth. "That's all a bit holy Joe-ish for me," said Short, who squirms under praise.
It is politics she worships with a quasi-religious passion -- not self or god or those who would do anything to win power.
"I love the Labour Party. Take all the tinsel away and it's that which I'm fighting for: a just and better country."
WOMEN'S SUPPORT
Women, especially, are magnetised by Short, who made her name campaigning against the daily diet of semi-naked women splayed in Britain's best-selling Sun newspaper.

"The Page Three girls are still there so it didn't work but at least the argument shifted. I got some vile mail -- porn with my head stuck on -- but 10,000 letters of support is boxes and boxes full. It produced massively my biggest postbox," she said.
Poor women, old women, tired and downtrodden women all team around the MP as she blitzes a cut-priced shopping mall.
"Just to see her face, just to see her face," says one supporter, hovering nearby. Another woman, short and fat, plasters Short with kisses before pledging support:
"We've always been chasing you. We've watched every word that's come out of your mouth. To us -- you're it."
Says Short: "It makes me feel quite humble. I've never met her yet I'm a feature of her life. That's quite moving."

Much in life moves Short -- not least the son she met last year after a 31-year hiatus. Short gave up Toby Graham for adoption when he was six weeks old and endured non-stop "pain and loss" until they were very publicly reunited last year.
She was too young, too poor and too confused to keep him, says Short, though it is a decision she bitterly regrets.
"When they came to take him it was terrible. It's been terrible ever since," Short said last year.
Nation, party and friends were stunned -- and not even her harshest political foe could help but wish Short well in her new-found role as mother of one and grandmother of two.
At the time Short said it was like falling in love without all the complications. Had the honeymon now ended?

"No, we're still wonderful. We just get on enormously well. The power of our mutual regard and affection had complications for other people but that's been worked through and it's bliss," said Short. "It's so precious."
